A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their main text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 1–4 report original inference experiments on election-survey and proteomics data using simulated strategic annotators.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original sentinel-identifiability, utility-misspecification, and continuous-income regression results in Appendices B and D.

M1.justification: The core sentinel mechanism, estimators, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged. Appendix C sketches an adaptation with difficulty-specific auditing, accuracy, bonuses, and construction costs, plus allocation first across difficulty classes and then within each class. A complete optimal policy is left to future work.

E1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds California 2019 ACS PUMS data and estimation of the age coefficient in continuous-income regression, extending evaluation beyond binary survey responses and protein properties. The new sensitivity experiments also introduce partially identifiable sentinels and misspecified worker responses.

E2.justification: The new Figure 3 explicitly compares the posterior-belief variant against the nominal incentive-robust method, alongside classical, uniform, and active. The original benchmark comparator sets are retained. The revised description of classical agrees with its existing formula in v1 Appendix B, so it does not establish a replacement baseline.

E3.justification: New sensitivity protocols set the worker's sentinel belief to 0.8ρ and simulate actual utility μ(b)=kb, with k drawn uniformly from 0.25 to 0.75 while design assumes μ(b)=b. ACS adds squared-loss regression-coefficient inference. These are focused protocol additions; the original benchmark procedures are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix B and Appendix D.1 add direct sensitivity tests of two central assumptions: sentinel indistinguishability and correctly specified worker behavior. Figures 3–4 examine whether inference advantages survive these departures, providing robustness evidence absent from v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report representative confidence intervals, average interval widths, and empirical coverage. v2 extends this reporting to additional Monte Carlo experiments without introducing a different uncertainty-estimation procedure, run counts, seeds, or significance tests.

E6.justification: New Figures 3–5 report interval-width and coverage results for imperfect sentinel beliefs, utility misspecification, and ACS regression. Figure 3 shows deterioration relative to ideal sentinel beliefs while retaining advantages over the external baselines. All original figure results and the approximately 80% survey and 70% protein budget-saving statements are retained.

T1.justification: Section 5.1 corrects label probabilities to use q(e), and the M-estimation population loss and related assumptions explicitly use ground-truth labels. Appendix B adds a posterior-belief incentive equation; Appendix C adds difficulty-dependent definitions and a budget constraint. The principal theorems and proof arguments remain largely unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract newly foregrounds the general accuracy-based-payment impossibility, but this claim already appears in v1's introduction and Section 3. The core contributions—sentinel incentives, joint auditing and sampling, inference guarantees, and improved budget efficiency—retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: New discussion explains sentinel detectability, failure when ordinary tasks receive zero posterior sentinel probability, and the tradeoff between detectable and excessively obvious continuous-label perturbations. It also discusses behavioral misspecification and incomplete characterization of heterogeneous policies. Section 4 corrects the interpretation of q(e) as conditional correction probability rather than overall output accuracy.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a study-specific experimental code address in Appendix D, whereas v1 links only the upstream active-inference codebase. It also documents the new sensitivity settings and ACS target and covariates. The original pseudocode, label simulation, and baseline correction formulas are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to labeling platforms, annotation applications, and the ACS data source, including Labelbox, Label Studio, Cormier, Qiao, Artemova, and Ding. Positioning relative to Bastani and Cachon and to active statistical inference remains essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction receive localized expansion, related work and experimental descriptions are condensed, and sentinel construction receives additional explanation. Equal-contribution and conflict-of-interest disclosures are added. New appendices precede the former experiment appendix, but the central narrative and section sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds three multipanel figures displaying the two sensitivity analyses and continuous-outcome experiment, substantially expanding the visual evidence. Original plots are preserved and relocated: v1 Figure 3 becomes v2 Figure 7, and v1 Figure 4 becomes v2 Figure 6. Budget-saving plots are consolidated in the appendix.

improvement.justification: v2 broadens v1's binary-outcome, idealized evaluation with continuous regression and tests of two practical assumptions. Explicit failure conditions, mathematical corrections, and study-specific code information improve clarity and assessability. The gain is limited because the added robustness claims extend beyond the narrow simulations, while the heterogeneous-policy extension remains a sketch.
